name: Seventeen Names for Leaving
description: Composed in 2183 by Idris Mwangi-Thorsen during the first year of GLMZ's great consolidation, when entire Shelf neighborhoods were being demolished to make way for Circuit expansion and thousands of families were displaced or disappeared in the chaos. The song lists, across seventeen verses, seventeen different words for departure drawn from seventeen different languages spoken by GLMZ's diaspora population — none of them are the word for 'death,' but every one of them means it, obliquely. Musically it is built on a slow, cycling pentatonic figure played on a modified erhu over hand drum patterns that echo Yoruba funeral percussion, with a chorus that requires a minimum of four voices to perform correctly.
creator: Idris Mwangi-Thorsen
audience: Shelf and Circuit communities primarily, especially families displaced during the Consolidation era; sung at funerals, memorials, and demolition vigils across Tiers 1-3
cultural_impact: No other song in GLMZ functions so specifically as a Shelf funeral standard. Mwangi-Thorsen, who died in 2201 in a Shelf tenement fire, never recorded it commercially — it exists only in live performance tradition and in dozens of amateur recordings of varying quality circulated on pirate feeds. The song is considered semi-sacred in many Shelf communities; there are families who have been singing it at every death for three generations. Its use spread upward into Tier 2 and 3 communities as the Consolidation's effects widened. Vantablack Media once attempted to license and produce a commercial version; the recording session was abandoned when studio musicians reportedly refused to continue.
known_fans: displaced families from the Consolidation era
pirate radio stations that play it at dawn
story_hooks: The players attend a funeral in the Shelf and hear the song performed by a woman who claims to be Mwangi-Thorsen's daughter — but Mwangi-Thorsen was recorded as having no children, and the woman knows verses no surviving recording contains.

A Vantablack Media executive wants to license the song for a corporate memorial campaign honoring workers 'lost' in a factory disaster the company caused — the players are hired either to facilitate or to stop it.

One of the seventeen words in the song turns out to be a fragment of a language that has been entirely erased from official GLMZ records, and a linguist believes the full lexicon may still exist somewhere in the Shelf.
